## What this exercise is about

This exercise groups the 55 townships of Shan State in Myanmar into regions with similar access to information and communication technology. The grouping uses six household ICT measures from the 2014 census, radio, television, land line phone, mobile phone, computer and internet at home.

Planners often want regions that are both homogeneous and joined together on the map. Ordinary cluster analysis only looks at the first condition. The second half of the exercise adds the map back in, first with SKATER, which cuts a minimum spanning tree of neighbouring townships, and then with ClustGeo, which lets me choose how much weight geography gets.

The work is split into six parts. Part 1 explores the variables with charts and choropleth maps, Part 2 checks correlations, and Part 3 runs hierarchical clustering. Part 4 and Part 5 cover the two spatially constrained methods, and Part 6 profiles the clusters.

## Setting up

### The data

Two datasets come from the Myanmar Information Management Unit (MIMU).

The first is `myanmar_township_boundaries`, an ESRI shapefile with the polygon boundary of every township in Myanmar. The second is `Shan-ICT.csv`, an extract of the 2014 Myanmar Population and Housing Census at township level. It has the number of households in each township and the number that own each of the six ICT items.

I put the shapefile in `data/geospatial` and the csv in `data/aspatial`, and added an empty `data/rds` folder for the intermediate files. The notes use `chap12/data/...`, and I changed every path to match this folder layout.

### Packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(spdep, tmap, sf, ClustGeo, 
               ggpubr, cluster, factoextra, NbClust,
               heatmaply, corrplot, psych, tidyverse, GGally)
```
:::


The packages fall into five groups. **sf** and **spdep** handle the spatial data, and **tidyverse** covers readr, dplyr, tidyr and ggplot2 for the attribute data. **tmap** draws the choropleth maps. **corrplot**, **ggpubr**, **heatmaply**, **psych** and **GGally** are used to visualise the variables, and **cluster**, **factoextra**, **NbClust** and **ClustGeo** run the cluster analysis.

::: {.callout-note}
## rgdal is no longer needed

The package list in the notes mentions **rgdal**. It was retired from CRAN in 2023, and sf now does all of its reading and writing work, so I left it out. The `p_load()` call in the notes already does not include it.
:::

### Deriving penetration rates

The raw counts mostly measure how big a township is. A township with many households will also have many households with a radio, and that says nothing about how common radios are there. I divided each count by the total number of households and multiplied by 1,000 to get the number of owning households per thousand.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ict_derived <- ict %>%
  mutate(`RADIO_PR` = `Radio`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`TV_PR` = `Television`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`LLPHONE_PR` = `Land line phone`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`MPHONE_PR` = `Mobile phone`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`COMPUTER_PR` = `Computer`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  mutate(`INTERNET_PR` = `Internet at home`/`Total households`*1000) %>%
  rename(`DT_PCODE` =`District Pcode`,`DT`=`District Name`,
         `TS_PCODE`=`Township Pcode`, `TS`=`Township Name`,
         `TT_HOUSEHOLDS`=`Total households`,
         `RADIO`=`Radio`, `TV`=`Television`, 
         `LLPHONE`=`Land line phone`, `MPHONE`=`Mobile phone`,
         `COMPUTER`=`Computer`, `INTERNET`=`Internet at home`) 
```

## Part 1, Exploratory data analysis

### Distribution of radio ownership

A histogram shows the overall shape of a variable, and a boxplot picks out outliers. I started with the raw count of households with a radio.

### Joining the census data to the boundaries

The choropleth maps need the rates attached to the polygons. `left_join()` keeps `shan_sf` as the base, so the result is still an sf object, and adds the columns of `ict_derived` by matching `TS_PCODE`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf, 
                     ict_derived, by=c("TS_PCODE"="TS_PCODE"))
  
write_rds(shan_sf, "data/rds/shan_sf.rds")
```
:::


All 55 township codes match in both directions, so no township is dropped or left without data.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why TS.x and TS.y appear

The notes mention a message naming the join field. With `by` written out there is no message. Both tables have `DT`, `DT_PCODE` and `TS` columns besides the key, so dplyr keeps both copies and adds the suffixes `.x` and `.y`. I checked that `TS.x` and `TS.y` hold the same township name in all 55 rows. That is why the later code refers to `TS.x`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shan_sf <- read_rds("data/rds/shan_sf.rds")
```
:::


### Choropleth map of the radio penetration rate

`qtm()` gives a quick map with default settings.


::: {.cell}


::: {.cell-output-display}

Radio ownership is highest in the west of Shan South and Shan North. Ywangan, Pindaya and Lawksawk near Taunggyi and Mabein in the north west all exceed 380 per thousand. The lowest rates are in the north east along the Chinese border, Konkyan and Laukkaing in the Kokang area at 21 and 53, and Narphan and Pangwaun in the Wa area at about 75.

### Counts versus rates on the map

To show how much the counts depend on township size, I mapped total households next to the number of radio households. The notes use tmap v3 syntax here, and I translated it to v4, where the classification goes into `tm_scale_intervals()`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "TT_HOUSEHOLDS",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Total households")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

RADIO.map <- tm_shape(shan_sf) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "RADIO",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Number Radio")) + 
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5) 

tmap_arrange(TT_HOUSEHOLDS.map, RADIO.map,
             asp=NA, ncol=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


The two maps look almost the same. Taunggyi and Lashio are in the top class on both, and the correlation between total households and radio households across the 55 townships is 0.94.

Next I put total households next to the rate. The notes do this with two variables in one `tm_polygons()` call and `tm_facets(sync = TRUE)`. In v4, a vector of variables in `fill` already produces facets, and `fill.free = TRUE` gives each one its own Jenks classes.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(shan_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "RADIO_PR"),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "jenks"),
              fill.free = TRUE,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_facets(ncol = 2) +
  tm_layout(outer.margins = 0, asp = 0)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=1152}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## Translating the tmap v3 code

Three changes were needed for tmap 4.4. `tm_fill(col = ..., n = 5, style = "jenks", title = ...)` became `tm_polygons(fill = ..., fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = ...))`. `tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)` became `tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)`, since a border is a line. `tm_legend(legend.position = ...)` was replaced by a position inside the `fill.legend` argument.
:::

The course asks whether I can see the differences. The rate map breaks the link with size. Taunggyi, the largest township, drops to the fourth of five classes for `RADIO_PR`, and Lashio, the second largest, falls to the middle class at 236 per thousand. Small townships such as Mabein (8,632 households) and Monghpyak (6,165) move into the top class. The correlation between total households and `RADIO_PR` is only 0.34, which confirms that the rate measures something different from size.

## Part 2, Correlation analysis

Cluster analysis treats each variable as a separate dimension. Two variables that carry almost the same information would count that information twice, so I checked the correlations between the six rates first.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cluster_vars.cor = cor(ict_derived[,12:17])
corrplot.mixed(cluster_vars.cor,
         lower = "ellipse", 
               upper = "number",
               tl.pos = "lt",
               diag = "l",
               tl.col = "black")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex06_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


`COMPUTER_PR` and `INTERNET_PR` have the strongest correlation, 0.87, so I keep only one of them. Following the notes, I keep `COMPUTER_PR`. The next highest pairs are `MPHONE_PR` with `COMPUTER_PR` at 0.74 and `TV_PR` with `MPHONE_PR` at 0.72. They are high but well below 0.87, and the notes keep all of them.

Radio stands apart from the rest. Its correlation with the other rates ranges from -0.31 with land line phones to 0.24 with television. Radio is common in townships where the more modern items are rare, so it adds information the other variables do not have.

### Selecting the optimal clustering algorithm

`agnes()` from **cluster** works like `hclust()` but also returns the agglomerative coefficient. It measures how strong the clustering structure is, and values closer to 1 mean a stronger structure. I computed it for four methods.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
m <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c( "average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730 
```


:::
:::


Ward's method has the highest coefficient at 0.943, ahead of complete linkage at 0.895, average at 0.813 and single linkage at 0.663. Single linkage chains townships one at a time, which gives the weakest structure. I use Ward's method from here on.

### Determining the optimal number of clusters

The notes list three common methods for choosing the number of clusters, the elbow method, the average silhouette method and the gap statistic, and use the gap statistic.

#### Gap statistic method

The gap statistic compares the within cluster variation for each k with the value expected from data with no cluster structure. The best k is the one with the largest gap. `clusGap()` from **cluster** computes it, and `hcut()` from **factoextra** does the hierarchical clustering inside each run.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict, 
                    FUN = hcut, 
                    nstart = 25, 
                    K.max = 10, 
                    B = 50)
# Print the result
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")
```

### Interpreting the dendrogram

Each leaf of the dendrogram is one township. Similar townships are joined into branches lower down, and the height of a fusion shows how different the two groups are. ## Part 4, Spatially constrained clustering with SKATER

SKATER (Spatial 'K'luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal) only allows neighbouring townships to join the same cluster. It links all townships in a minimum spanning tree, where each link is between two neighbours, and then cuts the tree into pieces. Each piece is one cluster and is contiguous by construction.

### Converting to SpatialPolygonsDataFrame

The notes convert `shan_sf` into an sp object because older versions of the SKATER functions only accepted sp.

### Computing the minimum spanning tree

#### Calculating edge costs

`nbcosts()` gives each neighbour link a cost, the euclidean distance between the two townships in the five ICT variables. A low cost means two neighbours have similar profiles.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lcosts <- nbcosts(shan.nb, shan_ict)
```
:::


I then turned the neighbour list into a weights object with these costs as the weights. Style `"B"` keeps the costs as they are, without row standardisation.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, 
                   lcosts, 
                   style="B")
summary(shan.w)
```

```{.r .cell-code}
r_squared <- function(cl) {
  x <- as.matrix(shan_ict)
  tss <- sum(sweep(x, 2, colMeans(x))^2)
  wss <- sum(sapply(unique(cl), function(g) {
    xg <- x[cl == g, , drop = FALSE]
    sum(sweep(xg, 2, colMeans(xg))^2)
  }))
  1 - wss / tss
}

c(hclust = r_squared(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER),
  skater = r_squared(ccs6))
```

```

0.7610272 0.4998530 
```


:::
:::


The hierarchical clusters explain 76 percent of the variance in the five variables, and the SKATER clusters only 50 percent.

::: {.callout-important}
## My takeaway

SKATER turned the scattered pieces into three large connected regions, west, centre and eastern border, plus three tiny clusters for townships too unusual to fit anywhere. That contiguity cost a lot of homogeneity, with the explained variance falling from 76 to 50 percent. Asking for six clusters did not give six useful regions here, because three of the five cuts went into trimming outliers.

## Part 5, Spatially constrained clustering with ClustGeo

**ClustGeo** offers a softer constraint. Its `hclustgeo()` function runs a Ward-like hierarchical clustering on two dissimilarity matrices at once. D0 holds the differences in the clustering variables and D1 holds the differences in space. A mixing parameter alpha between 0 and 1 sets the balance. At alpha = 0 only D0 counts, and at alpha = 1 only geography counts. The aim is to find an alpha that makes the clusters more compact on the map without losing too much homogeneity in the variables, and `choicealpha()` helps with that.

### Ward-like hierarchical clustering with ClustGeo

With only D0, `hclustgeo()` is an ordinary Ward clustering. D0 has to be a `dist` object, so I reused `proxmat`.

Cluster 4 stands out with the highest television and mobile phone ownership, and it also leads on land lines and computers. These are the six border and trade towns, Muse, Tachileik, Laukkaing, Mongla, Namhkan and Taunggyi.

Cluster 5 has the lowest television, mobile phone and computer rates of all six clusters. The notes say it is lowest on all five items, but cluster 6 has less radio and cluster 2 has fewer land lines.

`scale = "globalminmax"` draws the raw values on one shared axis. `ggparcoord()` offers five other options. `std` subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, and `robust` subtracts the median and divides by the median absolute deviation. `uniminmax` rescales each variable to run from 0 to 1. `center` applies uniminmax and then centres each variable on a summary value set by `scaleSummary`, and `centerObs` does the same around one chosen observation set by `centerObsID`.

With `globalminmax`, television and mobile phones fill most of the height and computers are squashed along the bottom. I also drew the same plot with `uniminmax`, which puts every variable on the same 0 to 1 range.

## Wrapping up

The five ICT rates group Shan State's 55 townships into six profiles that range from a connected urban group to a group with very low ownership of every item. Without a spatial constraint these profiles are scattered across the state in 24 to 28 separate pieces. SKATER produced three connected regions, west, centre and eastern border, plus three outlier clusters, at the cost of explaining only 50 percent of the variance. ClustGeo with alpha = 0.2 kept 65 percent, made most clusters compact, and left the main towns together as one scattered urban group.
